name: DO BRUSSEL BURGER - (Comes with brussel sprouts)

recipe.history:
Brussels sprouts (Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera) trace their cultivated origins to the Low Countries of northern Europe, with the earliest reliable written records appearing in Belgium around the 13th century. The vegetable takes its name from Brussels, the Belgian capital, where it was widely grown in the surrounding agricultural regions during the 16th and 17th centuries. Flemish and Dutch farmers refined the plant through selective cultivation, favoring tight, compact heads that could withstand the cold, damp winters of the region. By the 18th century, Brussels sprouts had spread steadily through France and Britain, carried along trade routes and into kitchen gardens of the landed gentry, who prized them as a late-season green when other vegetables had long since been spent by frost.

Brussels sprouts arrived in North America with European settlers, with Thomas Jefferson among the first to document growing them at Monticello in the early 1800s. For much of American culinary history, they were boiled into submission — grey, sulfurous, and deeply resented by generations of children at holiday tables. The vegetable's American rehabilitation began in earnest in the late 1990s and accelerated through the 2000s, when chefs discovered that high-heat roasting and pan-charring transformed their flavor entirely, caramelizing natural sugars and driving off the bitter glucosinolate compounds responsible for their bad reputation. From gastropub menus to fast-casual burger joints, crispy Brussels sprouts emerged as a bold, unexpected topping — their nutty, slightly smoky char providing a counterpoint to rich beef fat in a way that pickles and onions simply cannot.

I remember the first time I put Brussels sprouts on a burger. It was a Tuesday, late autumn, the kind of evening where the light dies before dinner and the kitchen feels like the only warm room in the world. I had a cast iron pan going with a little bacon fat left over from breakfast, and a bowl of halved sprouts I'd meant to roast as a side. On impulse I threw them in the pan, let them sit undisturbed until they screamed and blistered, then hit them with a splash of apple cider vinegar that sent a cloud of steam hissing toward the ceiling. I put them on a medium rare patty almost as an afterthought. The first bite stopped me cold — the char, the acid, the grass-fed beef, the soft give of a buttered bun all arriving at once. I stood at the counter and finished the whole thing before I thought to sit down. Some combinations you stumble into. Some stumble into you.

Medium rare is not a preference. It is a philosophy. A beef patty cooked to an internal temperature of 130–135°F (54–57°C) retains its moisture, its fat stays liquid rather than rendered out onto the grill grates, and the myoglobin in the muscle fibers holds just enough structure to give the meat a tender, yielding resistance that well-done beef can never replicate. The pink center is not a sign of carelessness — it is evidence of restraint, of knowing when to pull back, of trusting the meat to finish what the heat started. Every great burger is an exercise in not overdoing it. The bun should be toasted, not burned. The sauce should complement, not bury. The toppings should contrast, not compete. And the patty, always, should be medium rare. To cook it further is to lose the point entirely.
ingredients: 300g (2½ cups) bread flour, plus extra for dusting
3 large eggs, room temperature (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
85g (6 tbsp) unsalted butter, softened and cubed
1 tbsp sesame seeds (optional, for topping buns)
680g (1½ lbs) freshly ground beef, 80/20 chuck blend
½ tsp freshly cracked black pepper
1 tbsp neutral oil (such as canola or grapeseed) for the cooking surface
450g (1 lb) Brussels sprouts, tough outer leaves removed, halved lengthwise
2 tbsp rendered bacon fat or unsalted butter
Kosher salt and black pepper to taste
3 strips thick-cut bacon, cut into lardons
1 large ripe tomato, sliced into 4 thick rounds
½ red onion, thinly sliced into rings
2 tbsp unsalted butter, for toasting buns
instructions: 1. Make the brioche buns: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with a dough hook. Add 2 eggs and the warm milk. Mix on low for 2 minutes until shaggy, then increase to medium and knead for 5 minutes.

2. With the mixer running on medium-low, add the softened butter one cube at a time, waiting until each piece is fully incorporated before adding the next. Once all butter is added, increase to medium-high and knead for 8–10 minutes until the dough is smooth, elastic, and pulls away cleanly from the bowl sides.
3. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise at room temperature for 1–1.5 hours until doubled in size.

4. Punch down the dough and divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 130g each). Shape each into a tight ball by pulling the surface taut and pinching at the bottom. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing 3 inches apart. Cover loosely and let rise again for 45–60 minutes until noticeably puffed.

5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Beat the remaining egg with 1 tbsp water and brush gently over each bun. Sprinkle with sesame seeds if using. Bake for 16–18 minutes until deep golden brown. Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely before slicing.

6. Make the roasted garlic aioli: While buns bake, place unpeeled garlic cloves on a small square of foil, drizzle with 1 tsp olive oil, wrap tightly, and roast alongside the buns for 25 minutes until soft and golden. Squeeze the roasted garlic from its skins and mash into a smooth paste.

7. Whisk together egg yolks, Dijon mustard, and lemon juice in a medium bowl until combined. Very slowly drizzle in the neutral oil drop by drop while whisking constantly — this builds the emulsion. Once the mixture thickens and roughly half the oil is incorporated, you can add the remaining neutral oil in a thin, steady stream, whisking the entire time. Repeat with the extra-virgin olive oil.
8. Fold in the roasted garlic paste. Season with fine sea salt to taste. Refrigerate aioli until ready to assemble.

9. Prepare the Brussels sprouts: Cook bacon lardons in a large cast iron skillet over medium heat until crispy and the fat has rendered, about 6–7 minutes. Remove bacon with a slotted spoon and set aside, leaving the fat in the pan.

10. Increase heat to medium-high. Add Brussels sprouts cut-side down to the hot bacon fat in a single layer. Do not stir — let them sear undisturbed for 4–5 minutes until the cut faces are deeply charred and caramelized.

11. Toss the sprouts, add the butter or extra bacon fat if the pan looks dry, and cook for another 3–4 minutes until sprouts are tender through but still have bite. Add the red pepper flakes and stir for 30 seconds.

12. Deglaze the pan with apple cider vinegar — it will hiss and steam aggressively. Stir to lift any browned bits. Drizzle in the honey, toss to coat, and return the bacon lardons to the pan. Season with salt and pepper. Keep warm over very low heat.

13. Form the patties: Divide the ground beef into 4 equal portions (approximately 170g each). Handle as little as possible — overworking develops tough myosin bonds. Gently form each portion into a patty roughly ¾ inch thick and slightly wider than your buns (they will shrink during cooking). Press a shallow dimple into the center of each patty with your thumb to prevent doming.
14. Season both sides generously with kosher salt, black pepper, and garlic powder immediately before cooking — not in advance, as salt draws out moisture.

15. Heat a cast iron skillet or flat griddle over high heat until smoking, about 3–4 minutes. Add 1 tbsp neutral oil and swirl to coat. Place patties in the pan and do not move them for 3 minutes, allowing a crust to form.

16. Flip each patty once. Place a slice of Gruyère on each. Cook for an additional 2–3 minutes. Begin checking internal temperature at 2 minutes using an instant-read thermometer inserted through the side into the center of the patty. Pull patties off heat when they reach 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Tent loosely with foil and rest for 3 minutes — carryover cooking will bring them to a perfect 133–135°F.

17. Toast the buns: While patties rest, melt butter in the same pan over medium heat. Place buns cut-side down and toast for 1–2 minutes until golden and lightly crisp. Watch carefully — brioche browns quickly.

18. Assemble the burgers: Spread a generous layer of roasted garlic aioli on both the top and bottom bun. Layer butter lettuce on the bottom bun, followed by a tomato slice and red onion rings. Set the cheese-topped patty on the onions. Heap a generous portion of the warm Brussels sprouts and bacon mixture directly over the patty. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately.
